# Two-sided local mass variations and a compatible hull-bump obstruction

This is a scoped variational theorem. It does not classify an attained
mixed-integer depth minimizer or prove (OC). Its additional geometric
content is an exact construction of independently prescribed signed local
masses under a strict compatibility hypothesis, and an explicit obstruction
to outward mass localization when that hypothesis fails.

The all-circuit first-variation condition and signed smooth variations have
antecedents in `candidate 6a6bd3b533ab6973`,
`candidate 23c5cf376b5f9d55`, and
`candidate ed7be0e1efdfe13b`. The inward-only mass construction
and its inequality dual are in
`candidate a277c91b06544c90`.
The present construction needs neither an ambient uniformly convex defining
function, differentiability of the maximizing center, nor a differentiable
support perturbation in its mass parameter.

## 1. Setting and a quantitative open compatibility condition

Let P be a finite lattice-convex subset of Z^n, meaning
P=conv(P) intersect Z^n, with aff(P)=R^n. For n=0 take the one-point base
set. Let d>=1. For p in P let K_p be a full-dimensional compact convex body
in R^d. Suppose these are the actual fibers of

    C=conv union_(p in P) ({p} x K_p).

Then C is a convex body, and its nonempty integer fibers are exactly these.
Use the measure mu=sum_(p in P) vol_d on these fibers; put
M=mu(C)>0. All halfspaces below are closed ambient halfspaces.

For q in P form the coefficient polytope

    E_q={lambda_p>=0 (p!=q):
               sum_(p!=q)lambda_p=1,
               sum_(p!=q)lambda_p p=q}.

It can be empty. Say the family has **strict compatibility** if for every
extreme point lambda of every nonempty E_q,

    sum_(p!=q) lambda_p K_p is compactly contained in int K_q.       (1)

There are finitely many such constraints. Consequently there is kappa>0
such that each left side plus kappa B_d lies in K_q. If there are no
constraints, choose any positive kappa.

**Lemma 1 (open compatibility).** If convex bodies K'_p satisfy
d_H(K'_p,K_p)<eta<kappa/2 for all p, their convex hull over P has exactly
the fibers K'_p.

Proof. Write h_p for the support functions. For every unit u, every extreme
coefficient vector in E_q obeys

    sum lambda_p h_p(u)<=h_q(u)-kappa.

Every member of E_q is a convex combination of its extreme points, so the
same inequality holds for it. Hausdorff distance gives

    sum lambda_p h'_p(u)<=h'_q(u)-kappa+2eta<=h'_q(u).               (2)

A convex representation of q which uses q itself either is trivial or,
after cancelling its q coefficient, reduces to E_q. Thus (2) proves every
Minkowski inclusion necessary and sufficient for the q-section of the hull
to be K'_q. This proves the assertion simultaneously for all q. The
integer projection remains conv(P), so no unlisted integer fiber appears.

## 2. When an individual outward hull bump is local

Let K be a convex body in R^d. Suppose v in boundary K has a unique unit
supporting normal u, and its support face is a singleton:

    K intersect {x:u.x=h_K(u)}={v}.                              (3)

Fix h with u.h>0 and set a(t)=v+t h,

    K(t)=conv(K,a(t)),
    Delta(t)=|K(t)|-|K|.

**Lemma 2 (locality and exact mass inversion).** For t>0 sufficiently
small, Delta(t)>0. It is continuous and strictly increasing with
Delta(t)->0, and

    sup_{x in K(t)\K}|x-v| ->0 as t down to0.                    (4)

In particular there is a unique small t for each sufficiently small
prescribed added mass Delta.

Proof. Since u.a(t)>h_K(u), the hull strictly contains K. The hulls are
nested: a(s) is on [v,a(t)] when 0<s<t. Their u-support values are strictly
increasing. Strictly nested full-dimensional convex bodies have strictly
different volumes: a point outside the smaller compact body, combined
with an interior ball of the larger body, supplies a positive-volume
subset of their difference. Hausdorff continuity gives volume continuity
and the limit at zero.

To prove (4), suppose that t_i->0 and x_i in K(t_i)\K stay away from v.
Write x_i=(1-lambda_i)c_i+lambda_i a(t_i), with c_i in K and
0<lambda_i<=1. Take a unit normal n_i strictly separating x_i from K.
Then n_i.a(t_i)>h_K(n_i), so

    0<=h_K(n_i)-n_i.v<t_i |h|.

Pass to subsequences. Any limiting n supports K at v, hence equals u by
uniqueness. If lambda_i->1 then x_i->v already. Otherwise, after another
subsequence, 1-lambda_i is bounded below, and separation gives

    (1-lambda_i)(h_K(n_i)-n_i.c_i)
          <lambda_i(n_i.a(t_i)-h_K(n_i))<=t_i |h|.

Every limiting c_i therefore lies in the face (3), hence equals v. Again
x_i->v, a contradiction. This proves locality. The continuous strictly
increasing mass function has the claimed inverse.

Smoothness alone is insufficient: a relative-interior point of a flat
facet has a unique normal but not the singleton face in (3). A polytope
vertex generally fails the unique-normal condition. A smooth strictly
convex boundary point satisfies both conditions.

### 2.1 Several outward bumps in one fiber

Choose distinct points v_1,...,v_s of K satisfying Lemma 2, with their
directions h_i and exterior points a_i(t_i). For each define its closed
visible-normal set

    N_i(t_i)={n in S^(d-1): n.a_i(t_i)>=h_K(n)}.

As t_i->0, these sets approach the singleton {u_i}: any sequence of their
normals has a limit supporting K at v_i. The normals u_i are distinct;
otherwise their common support face would contain two different points,
contrary to (3). Therefore for all sufficiently small positive t_i the
sets N_i(t_i) are pairwise disjoint.

**Lemma 3 (exact disjoint union).** For those parameters,

    conv(K,a_1,...,a_s)\K
             is the disjoint union of conv(K,a_i)\K.              (5)

Proof. Write L for the larger hull. An exterior boundary point y of L
belongs to an exposed face for some supporting normal n. That face must
contain at least one added point: otherwise it is contained in K. An
added point belonging to that face satisfies n.a_i=h_L(n)>=h_K(n), hence
n lies in N_i. At most one added point can belong to the face. The face
is consequently contained in conv(K,a_i), so y is in that single hull.
Any point x in L\K is on the segment from a fixed interior point of K to
an exterior boundary point y of L. The same single hull contains the
segment, so x is in the right side of (5).

Finally, if x were outside K and in two of the single hulls, a normal
strictly separating x from K would satisfy both n.a_i>h_K(n) and
n.a_j>h_K(n), contradicting disjointness of N_i and N_j. This proves (5).

In particular the masses of these single-point additions add exactly,
without an unmeasured bridge region between bumps.

## 3. An actual mixed source with arbitrary signed local masses

Retain strict compatibility (1). Choose a finite collection of distinct
measured points w_i=(p_i,v_i) such that:

* w_i is exposed in C by an ambient functional ell_i with unique maximizer
  w_i;
* v_i satisfies (3) and has a unique supporting normal in its own K_p_i.

Fix outward directions h_i as in Lemma 2. These are explicit hypotheses,
not properties asserted for all attained minimizers. Points can share a
base. Fix any vector xi=(xi_i) of real numbers.

**Theorem 4 (signed mass localization).** For all sufficiently small
epsilon>0 there is an actual convex body C_epsilon with the same positive
integer fibers P, converging fiberwise to C, with

    mu(C_epsilon)=M+epsilon sum_i xi_i.                            (6)

The signed measure difference is a sum of disjoint pieces supported in
neighborhoods shrinking to w_i, each having signed mass epsilon xi_i.
For every fixed finite collection of caps whose boundaries avoid all w_i,

    mu(C_epsilon intersect H)-mu(C intersect H)
                     =epsilon sum_i xi_i 1_H(w_i)                 (7)

for all sufficiently small epsilon. The identity remains valid if those
cap thresholds are moved by O(epsilon).

Proof. For xi_i>0, use Lemma 2's inverse to choose the unique t_i with
added own-fiber volume epsilon xi_i. In every affected fiber take the
convex hull of its original body and these exterior points. Lemma 3 makes
its additions disjoint with the prescribed masses. The new fiber bodies
are uniformly Hausdorff-close to their originals. Lemma 1 makes the whole
family actual. In fact their ambient hull is exactly

    L_epsilon=conv(C, (p_i,v_i+t_i h_i): xi_i>0),                   (8)

since each proposed fiber hull is generated by the displayed points and
the original fiber, and all proposed fibers are compatible.

For xi_i<0, move the exposing plane ell_i=h_i^* inward, where
h_i^*=ell_i(w_i). The other finitely many integer fibers have a strict
support gap, so a sufficiently small cut removes only part of K_p_i.
The original removed region approaches w_i. Its volume as a function of
cut depth is continuous and strictly increasing from zero: every interval
of sufficiently small levels contains a positive-volume slab of this
full-dimensional fiber. Invert it to remove exactly epsilon |xi_i|.

The finitely many original removed regions are disjoint. All positive
additions approach different selected points. For a negative point's
exposing functional these other selected points have a fixed strict gap;
its small trim therefore leaves every positive addition untouched. Define
C_epsilon to be (8) intersected with all these negative trim halfspaces.
The removed regions are exactly the prescribed original caps, and the
added regions are exactly the prescribed disjoint bumps. This proves (6)
and signed localization. Each fiber keeps an interior ball, so projection
and positivity persist. Its sections are actual by construction.

Every selected cap has a fixed nonzero margin at each w_i. Locality thus
places the complete corresponding changed piece strictly on that same
side for small epsilon. Moving its threshold by O(epsilon) cannot reach
these pieces. This proves (7), including its last assertion.

## 4. The equality dual for finite selected critical circuits

Let beta be the maximum normalized halfspace depth of the original source,
Q=beta M, and I its set of deepest bases. At each p in I select any one
positive critical circuit of actual ambient caps

    H_pj={ (q,x): a_pj.q+u_pj.x>=b_pj }, |u_pj|=1,
    mu(H_pj)=Q,
    sum_j rho_pj u_pj=0, rho_pj>0,

through a maximizing point of its anchor fiber. Assume the selected caps
avoid the finitely many points w_i in Theorem 4. Also assume their actual
left and right threshold slopes agree and are positive:

    F_pj(b_pj+s)=Q-S_pj s+o(|s|),  S_pj>0.                       (9)

These are conditions on the original caps; no boundary mass is deleted
from another fiber to manufacture (9). Proper cuts have these slopes;
coincident supporting facets must be checked using both traces.

Critical circuit covers and slack whole-fiber covers for nondeep bases
are supplied by the exact critical-cap lemmas in
`candidate b989614dc4f86228`. The relevant reason is
elementary: at the anchor base, the rho-weighted margins sum identically
to zero at every continuous x. Thus at least one closed cap contains each
x. Threshold shifts with rho-weighted sum zero retain this cover of the
ENTIRE continuous plane over that base.

Define

    kappa_pj=(rho_pj/S_pj)/sum_l(rho_pl/S_pl),
    A_pi=sum_j kappa_pj 1_H_pj(w_i).                            (10)

**Theorem 5 (signed descent and equality dual).** For each fixed real
vector xi the signed construction obeys

    limsup_(epsilon down to0)
      [D(C_epsilon)-beta]/epsilon
        <=(1/M) max_(p in I) sum_i xi_i(A_pi-beta).             (11)

Consequently at an unrestricted local minimum of D among actual positive
families on P there is a probability vector pi on the selected deepest
base circuits such that

    sum_(p in I) pi_p A_pi=beta for EVERY selected point i.     (12)

This conclusion holds for every finite selection allowed above. The
probability pi may depend on both the selected points and the selected
circuits; no one common stress for all circuits is asserted.

Proof. Set g_pj=sum_i xi_i 1_H_pj(w_i) and
a_p=sum_j kappa_pj g_pj=sum_i A_pi xi_i. Change the threshold of H_pj by

    delta b_pj=epsilon (g_pj-a_p)/S_pj.

Its circuit-weighted sum is exactly zero. Equations (7) and (9) give the
mass of every changed cap in this circuit as Q+epsilon a_p+o(epsilon).
The circuit still covers the entire plane at p. Nondeep bases have fixed
slack whole-plane covers; their cap masses change by only O(epsilon), so
their slack persists. These are therefore actual covers of every candidate
in every new fiber, including new points outside original fibers. Dividing
their maximum mass by (6) proves (11). This does not differentiate a chosen
center or exchange a maximum and a derivative.

At a local minimum the right side of (11) cannot be strictly negative for
any xi. Put r_p=(A_pi-beta)_i. Thus

    max_p r_p.xi>=0 for every real xi.                         (13)

The finite convex hull of the rows r_p must contain zero. Otherwise a
strict separating linear functional, with its sign chosen appropriately,
would make every r_p.xi<0, contradicting (13). Expressing zero as a convex
combination of the rows is exactly (12). This proves the equality dual.

Only nonnegative deletions were feasible in the inward-only theorem; its
dual had sum pi_p A_pi<=beta. The availability of every signed mass vector
here changes that inequality to equality. For a single deepest base it
forces the score of every selected critical circuit to equal beta at
every allowed selected point off its cap boundaries.

If the two threshold traces differ, one must instead use the separate
one-sided inverse-quantile formulas of
`candidate c9f582e034f0948d`. Replacing them by
one arbitrary section slope does not establish (11) or (12). A local
minimum restricted to at most N defining planes does not automatically
permit these hull additions and trims. The theorem concerns an unrestricted
local minimum, or another class explicitly containing these competitors.

## 5. Smooth own fibers do not ensure mixed mass localization

The strict compatibility in the preceding theorem cannot simply be omitted.
Here is an exact full-dimensional counterexample to that omission, for
every d>=2. It is an obstruction to an auxiliary localization claim, not
to (OC).

Let B=B_d be the unit Euclidean ball, V=|B|, and

    C=[0,2] x B,
    w=(0,e_1),
    w_t=(0,(1+t)e_1), t>0,
    C_t=conv(C,w_t).

All three original integer fibers are smooth strictly convex balls. The
point w is globally exposed by (z,x) -> x_1-z. Put

    K(t)=conv(B,(1+t)e_1),
    Delta_0=|K(t)|-V>0,
    Delta_1=|(K(t)+B)/2|-V.

The actual new fibers, with no approximation, are

    (C_t)_0=K(t),   (C_t)_1=(K(t)+B)/2,   (C_t)_2=B.            (14)

Indeed C_t is the convex hull of the endpoint bodies K(t) at base zero
and B at base two; a section at intermediate base z is their Minkowski
combination with weights 1-z/2 and z/2. The original middle ball is already
contained in that hull.

Brunn--Minkowski gives, with x=Delta_0/V>0,

    (V+Delta_1)/V
          >=[((1+x)^(1/d)+1)/2]^d
          >=1+x/2^d.                                        (15)

For the last inequality expand the dth power: its highest-power term is
1+x and every other term is at least its value at x=0. Thus

    Delta_1>=2^(-d) Delta_0.                                 (16)

Also (K(t)+B)/2 is contained in K(t), so Delta_1<=Delta_0. Consequently
at least the fixed fraction

    Delta_1/(Delta_0+Delta_1)>=1/(2^d+1)                      (17)

of ALL added mixed mass lies in the base-one fiber. This fiber has ambient
distance at least one from w. The normalized added mixed measures therefore
cannot converge to the point mass at w, although their own base-zero
addition does localize at w by Lemma 2. The compatibility constraint at
the middle base is active in the original family, with no strict margin.

### 5.1 Exact planar fraction

In dimension d=2 write a=1+t, theta=arccos(1/a), and
s=sqrt(a^2-1)=tan(theta). The two tangent segments from (a,0) to the unit
circle have length s. The removed circular boundary arc has angle 2theta.
The triangle over the chord has area s^3/a^2, whereas the disk cap over
that chord has area theta-s/a^2. Their difference is s-theta. Therefore

    Delta_0=s-theta>0,
    perimeter(K(t))=2pi+2(s-theta)=2pi+2Delta_0.               (18)

The planar parallel-body area identity, |K+B_2|=|K|+perimeter(K)+pi,
then gives exactly

    |(K(t)+B_2)/2|=pi+3Delta_0/4,
    Delta_1=3Delta_0/4.                                     (19)

Here the parallel-body identity follows by adjoining strips of width one
to the straight boundary segments and outer annular sectors to the
circular arcs; the normal-turn angles, including the two corners, sum to
2pi and give the pi term. Equivalently it is the elementary planar Steiner
formula. Thus the nonlocal proportion in this smooth own-fiber example is
EXACTLY 3/7 for every t>0.

### 5.2 Arbitrary integer dimension and absence of a heavy fiber

For n>=1 use

    C=[0,2] x [0,1]^(n-1) x B_d

and add the point ((0,0,...,0),(1+t)e_1). Its selected old point is exposed
by x_1-z_1-sum_(i=2)^n z_i. Every integer binary layer other than the all-zero
layer stays unchanged: an integer coordinate equal to one forces every
point in a convex representation to have that same coordinate, excluding
the added point. In the all-zero layer the exact fibers are still (14).
Thus (16)--(17) hold for every n>=1, with the same nonlocal distance.

Originally there are 3*2^(n-1) equal fibers of mass V. Each is strictly
less than M/2^n=3V/2, so this example lies outside the heavy-fiber sufficient
regime. For small t with Delta_0<V/4, every new fiber has mass at most
V+Delta_0<5V/4, whereas the new total divided by 2^n is at least 3V/2.
The perturbed family also has no heavy fiber.

The obstruction tracks actual other-fiber changes, uses the original
integer coordinates, and persists with smooth strictly convex own fibers.
It is exactly why a local outward-volume argument cannot be inferred from
ordinary fiber geometry without a compatibility analysis.
